extracted.intended_audience: literary theorists, dramatists, humorists, and students studying the nature and construction of comedy
extracted.subtask_description: Theoretical guidance for understanding and creating comic effect and comic character-types in drama and literature; explains the psychological and social sources of the laughable and methods for dramatizing them. Useful to writers, dramatists, and scholars designing or analysing comic characters and scenes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedy aims at the general / depiction of types
rubrics_metrics.description: ONLY one of all the arts that aims at the general ... Comedy depicts characters we have already come across and shall meet with again. It takes note of similarities. It aims at placing types before our eyes. It even creates new types, if necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design comic works around types/classes rather than unique individualities (contrast with tragedy). Use collective or type-based titling (examples: Le Misanthrope, Les Femmes savantes). After creating a central comic character, surround them with secondary characters who are simplified copies or satellites showing the same general traits, thereby establishing the type by repetition and variation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedy is midway between art and life; it has a corrective social aim
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedy lies midway between art and life. It is not disinterested as genuine art is. By organising laughter, comedy accepts social life as a natural environment, it even obeys an impulse of social life ... its scarcely confessed or scarcely conscious intention [is] to correct and instruct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When creating comic material, aim not only to please but to socialise/correct—laughter should expose and remedy social faults (e.g., vanity, separatism). Structure scenes so laughter functions as a corrective: it brings characters back to self-consciousness and readapts individuals into the social whole.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic observation is external and superficial (skin-deep)
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedy springs from an observation directed outwards. Settling on the surface, it will not be more than skin-deep, dealing with persons at the point at which they come into contact and become capable of resembling one another. It will go no farther.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep comic causes at an intermediate, observable level rather than deep psychological roots. Localise causes in a region of the soul that is visible to others (so the audience can recognise and laugh), and avoid penetrating too far into interiority which would rob the effect of laughability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideal comic type: required qualities (deep-rooted yet superficial, unconscious to owner, etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: An ideally comic character must be deep-rooted, so as to supply comedy with inexhaustible matter, and yet superficial, in order that it may remain within the scope of comedy; invisible to its actual owner ... visible to everybody else ... extremely considerate to its own self ... troublesome to others ... immediately repressible ... sure of reappearing under fresh aspects ... inseparable from social life ... capable of being tacked on to all the vices and even to a good many virtues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct characters who combine durability (repeatable trait) with surface-level expression and unconsciousness of the trait. Make the trait socially embedded so it recurs in varied contexts, is recognisable to others, reprievable by social correction, and adaptable to new comic permutations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vanity as a principal source of the comic
rubrics_metrics.description: This mixture is vanity. Probably there is not a single failing that is more superficial or more deep-rooted... The one failing that is essentially laughable is vanity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for manifestations of vanity (self-admiration, need for admiration) as fertile comic material. Show how vanity is simultaneously trivial and persistent; use its incongruity with reality to provoke laughter. Treat laughter itself as the social remedy for vanity—expose and deflate pretension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Professional/commercial types produce ready-made comic categories
rubrics_metrics.description: There are ready-made categories established by society itself ... the various trades, public services and professions ... the business of laughter is to repress any separatist tendency ... This we shall call the PROFESSIONAL COMIC. In the forefront we find professional vanity ... SOLEMNITY ... PROFESSIONAL CALLOUSNESS ... the device most in use ... is to confine [a profession] within the four corners of its own particular jargon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exploit professional habits, jargon, specialised logic, solemnity and callousness to create comic types. Translate professional terminology and modes of reasoning to inappropriate everyday contexts (examples: Molière's doctors, Femmes savantes) to reveal ludicrousness; contrast professional logic with common-sense situations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic logic: a special inversion of common sense (palpable absurdity)
rubrics_metrics.description: The comic is often a very special inversion of common sense ... it consists in seeking to mould things on an idea of one's own, instead of moulding one's ideas on things — in seeing before us what we are thinking of, instead of thinking of what we see (illustrated by Don Quixote seeing giants where others see windmills).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create absurd situations that arise from a character's fixed ideas or privileged recollections imposing themselves on perception. The absurdity should be specific: an inversion of normal adaptive intelligence (thinking leads perception rather than vice versa), producing a 'palpable' but character-driven absurdity that the audience recognises and laughs at.

rubrics_metrics.name: Universality lies in the effect produced (sincerity & convertive power)
rubrics_metrics.description: The universality here lies in the effect produced, and not in the cause... By the very effort it forces us to make against our predispositions in order to see sincerely. Sincerity is contagious. The efficacy of the lesson is the exact standard of the genuineness of the work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for comic truth that forces the audience to alter perception—works become 'universal' through their persuasive effect. Measure the success of comic writing by its power to compel recognition and imitation (i.e., the audience's willingness to accept the type as truthful), not by the objective generality of the cause.

rubrics_metrics.name: Build types by enumerating varieties and repetition (naturalist method)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the comic poet's object is to offer us types ... how can he set about it better than by showing us, in each instance, several different copies of the same model? That is just what the naturalist does in order to define a species. He enumerates and describes its main varieties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establish a comic type by presenting multiple instances/variants of the same trait; use repetition and comparative examples to abstract the essence of the type. Present satellites and variations to define the species and make the type recognizable and generalizable to the audience.
